title: Enhancing optical and electrical properties of PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites for advanced applications
abstract: Abstract The aim of this study is to investigate the synthesis and comprehensive characterization of Polyvinyl alcohol/Polyvinylpyrrolidone-Graphene nanoplatelet (PVA/PVP–GnP) nanocomposite films prepared using the solution mixing method. The structural, electrical, and optical properties of the films were evaluated, revealing significant enhancements in their physical properties attributed to the incorporation of GnPs. Electrical conductivity values dramatically increased from 1.96 × 10 –10  (for the pure PVA/PVP hybrid matrix) to 4.07 S m −1  (for the composite with 6.16 vol% GnP), due to the formation of conductive pathways created by the GnP network. Optical analysis demonstrated strong UV absorption, with a notable decrease in optical bandgap energy as GnP concentration increased, related to the creation of new localized energy states and charge transfer complexes. The Urbach energy, indicative of structural disorder and defect density, also increased with higher GnP content, reflecting enhanced electron transitions in the material. Refractive index, optical conductivity, and dielectric properties showed significant improvements, further supporting the potential of these materials for optoelectronic and photonic applications. The results emphasize the versatility of these nanocomposites for energy storage systems and other high-performance applications. Graphical abstract

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Polymeric nanocomposites have become a significant area of research in recent years due to their unique mechanical, electrical, thermal, and optical properties. These materials are widely used in various applications, ranging from optical and optoelectronic devices to drug delivery systems, owing to their biocompatibility, low cost, and ease of accessibility [ 1 ]. The development of nanocomposites is achieved by incorporating various nanomaterials into a polymer matrix, which enhances mechanical strength while maintaining the lightweight nature of the polymer and addressing its inherent limitations [ 2 ]. Moreover, the physicochemical advantages offered by nanomaterials—such as high surface area and reactivity—have broadened their application in energy conversion systems, including photovoltaic devices, sensors, and photonic technologies [ 3 ]. Due to their ease of production and environmental stability, polymeric nanocomposites stand out as promising candidates for the development of sustainable and high-performance materials [ 3 ].

Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) are considered ideal polymers for numerous technological applications owing to their biocompatibility, water solubility, and non-toxic nature [ 1 ]. Particularly, PVA exhibits excellent film-forming properties due to its semi-crystalline structure and ability to form hydrogen bonds, while the amorphous structure of PVP enhances the homogeneous distribution of additives, strengthening the stability of the polymer matrix [ 1 ,  4 ]. The blending of these two polymers enables the development of hybrid systems with improved mechanical, optical, and functional properties suitable for optoelectronic devices, sensors, and biomedical applications [ 5 ]. Furthermore, the hydrophilic nature and reactive functional groups of PVA allow easy crosslinking with dopants, while the high polarity and dielectric constant of PVP make it an excellent additive for solar cells, flexible coatings, and biomedical devices [ 6 ,  7 ].

Ongoing research in polymeric nanocomposites has reinforced the trend of blending different polymers to improve material performance and enable new applications. The scientific community is focusing on the development of hybrid polymer nanocomposites for diverse applications such as water purification, energy storage, sensing, and solar energy harvesting [ 4 ]. The solution casting method is widely preferred for preparing thin films, as it allows for homogeneous dispersion and enables the controlled combination of different polymers to produce materials with superior physical and chemical properties [ 4 ,  5 ]. These hybrid structures surpass the physical capabilities of materials composed of a single polymer type, enabling the design of more durable and functional systems [ 8 ]. In recent years, polymer blends have emerged as a strategic approach in technological device development, gradually replacing single-component polymers to yield more efficient and innovative materials [ 6 ].

Although PVA and PVP can be used in various applications, their inherent limitations restrict their performance in some cases. PVA suffers from low thermal stability and high water absorption capacity, which can reduce its mechanical strength and structural integrity, particularly under humid conditions [ 5 ]. Its low refractive index also limits its potential in optoelectronic applications [ 7 ]. PVP, on the other hand, has a brittle structure and limited mechanical strength, making it less suitable for flexible device fabrication [ 6 ]. Furthermore, both polymers exhibit low electrical conductivity, which hinders their use in electronic and energy storage applications [ 9 ]. To address these drawbacks, conductive fillers—especially carbon-based materials such as graphene and carbon nanotubes—are frequently incorporated. These fillers provide superior electrical conductivity, large surface area, and chemical stability, significantly improving the electrical, mechanical, and thermal performance of polymer composites [ 9 ]. However, ensuring compatibility between these nanomaterials and polymer matrices, achieving homogeneous dispersion, and preventing agglomeration remain major engineering challenges [ 2 ]. In polymer nanocomposites, the degree of nanoparticle–polymer interaction and the surface area of the filler are decisive factors governing the overall material properties [ 8 ].

In this context, the PVA/PVP blend has gained significant attention as a versatile and tunable host matrix for nanocomposites. The high miscibility of PVA and PVP arises from the strong hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl (–OH) groups of PVA and the carbonyl (C=O) groups of PVP [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. These interactions enhance the structural homogeneity and physicochemical stability of the blend. Studies have demonstrated that PVA and PVP form a thermodynamically miscible pair at all composition ratios [ 10 ,  13 ]. Both polymers are water-soluble and biocompatible, facilitating the preparation of homogeneous hybrid matrices and their modification with conductive nanofillers such as graphene nanoplatelets (GnP) [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]. The semicrystalline nature of PVA provides mechanical strength, while the amorphous PVP component reduces crystallinity, improving the optical and structural properties of the material [ 17 ,  18 – 19 ]. Moreover, PVP decreases the crystalline phase of PVA, imparting flexibility and amorphousness, whereas PVA acts as a plasticizer for PVP [ 20 ]. The synergistic combination of these polymers enhances optical transparency and electrical conductivity. The hydrogen bonding between PVA and PVP chains also enables strong interfacial interactions with nanofillers such as GnP [ 16 ,  21 ]. Consequently, the PVA/PVP matrix serves as an ideal platform for developing GnP-based nanocomposites with enhanced electrical and optical properties [ 14 ,  19 ,  22 ].

Graphene nanoplatelets (GnPs) stand out as a cost-effective alternative to single-layer graphene, offering high electrical and thermal conductivity along with excellent mechanical strength [ 23 ]. However, it should be noted that the optical and electrical properties of GnPs may be limited compared to those of single-layer graphene due to their multi-layered structure [ 24 ]. Although GnPs possess high specific surface areas, surface modification may sometimes be necessary to ensure adequate interaction with the polymer matrix. Additionally, unlike graphene oxide (GO), GnPs largely retain their optical, electrical, and mechanical properties by preserving their pristine basal plane structure [ 24 ]. In recent years, polymer-based nanocomposites have attracted significant interest across a wide range of applications—from optical filters to biosensors, and from fuel cells to high-performance dielectric materials [ 7 ]. The flexible nature of polymers makes them a suitable matrix for various nanomaterials, while the careful selection and dispersion of nanofillers enable the optimization of material properties. In this context, various factors—such as the shape, size, and concentration of nanoparticles—have been strategically utilized to enhance the optical, mechanical, and electrical performance of polymer nanocomposites [ 25 ].

Alsaif et al. [ 3 ] demonstrated that polyvinyl alcohol/manganese dioxide (PVA/MnO₂) nanomaterials could be useful in high-performance optoelectronic devices. Badawi and Alharthi [ 1 ] investigated the linear and nonlinear optical and electrical properties of reduced graphene oxide/cobalt-doped titanium dioxide (rGO/Co:TiO 2 )-doped PVP/PVA nanocomposites, demonstrating their potential for effective integration into optoelectronic applications. In another study, incorporating Sb 2 S 3  chalcogenide nanopowder into the PVA/PVP hybrid matrix was shown to significantly enhance the optical properties [ 5 ]. Mohamed et al. [ 26 ] focused on determining the optimal doping levels in poly(vinyl alcohol)/poly(vinyl pyrrolidone)/(polyethylene glycol)/zinc tungstate/polyaniline (PVA/PVP/PEG/ZnWO 4 /PANi) nanocomposites for use in optoelectronic and energy storage applications. Similarly, Soliman et al. [ 7 ] proposed the use of PVA/Bi-Ni oxide-rGO nanocomposites in optical device applications by enhancing their optical properties.

sections.heading: Material and method
paragraphs: Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, P8136, Sigma-Aldrich) with a density of 1.19–1.31 g cm −3 , melting point of 250 °C, viscosity of 4–6 cP (4% in H 2 O at 20 °C, lit.), average molecular weight of 30,000–70,000, and a hydrolysis degree of approximately 87–90% was used. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP K30, 81,420, Sigma-Aldrich) with a pH of 5.0–8.0 (10 g/L at 20 °C) and a density of 1.20 g cm −3  was also employed. Graphene nanoplatelets (GnP, 900413, Sigma-Aldrich) possessing an oxygen content below 1%, a specific surface area of 120–150 m 2  g −1 , an average thickness of 6–8 nm, a particle size of 25 µm, a melting point of 3652 °C, and a density of 2.2 g cm −3  were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. All material specifications were obtained from the manufacturer’s technical data sheets available on the official Sigma-Aldrich website.

All measurements were performed using three identical nanocomposite films for each  ϕ  value. During the measurements, the laboratory temperature was maintained at 24–25 °C and relative humidity of 55–60%. The electrical conductivities of the PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites were measured using a Keithley 6517A electrometer, which complies with the ASTM-D257 standard and employs alternating polarity method. A Varian Cary 100 Bio Model UV–Visible spectrometer, fabricated by Varian Instruments, Australia, was used to determine the UV–Vis absorbance and reflectance spectra in the wavelength range of 190 to 600 nm. The FTIR spectra of the samples were obtained using a Perkin Elmer Frontier spectrometer within the wavenumber range of 4000–500 cm −1 , aiming to determine the characteristic functional groups and potential interactions between the polymer matrix and the incorporated nanofillers. The surface morphology of the PVA/PVP hybrid matrix and the PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposite films was examined using a scanning electron microscope (Thermo Scientific Scios 2 DualBeam).

sections.heading: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis of the nanocomposites
paragraphs: The SEM images of the PVA/PVP hybrid matrix and the PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites are presented in Fig.  1 . The images show that the PVA/PVP hybrid matrix film exhibits a typically homogeneous polymer-blend morphology. In Fig.  1 a, the surface appears generally smooth, continuous, and free of prominent macropores at a magnification of 10 kx. This morphology indicates a compatible mixing of the polymer chains, supporting the good interaction and phase compatibility between PVA and PVP. The small particulate features and slight protrusions observed locally on the surface may be associated with microscale condensations or local drying effects within the polymer matrix; however, these features are not significant enough to compromise the integrity of the structure. At a higher magnification of 50 kx Fig.  1 b, the matrix exhibits a compact, dense, and non-porous microstructure, with no evident phase separation—consistent with the high miscibility of PVA and PVP. The surface roughness is also observed to be on the nano- to microscale. In Fig.  1 c, the platelet-like structures embedded within the PVA/PVP hybrid matrix are not strongly pronounced, indicating that the GnP sheets are well dispersed. The absence of distinct gaps or large voids at the polymer–filler interface suggests good interfacial interaction between the matrix and the GnP. Figure  1 d shows that, with increasing GnP content, a larger number of GnP platelets become visible, randomly distributed and in contact with one another. The morphology and distribution of the GnP sheets play a significant role in influencing the physical properties of the nanocomposite. Figure 1 SEM images of the PVA/PVP hybrid matrix at magnifications of  a  10 k and  b  50 k, as well as those of the PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites with GnP loadings of  c ϕ  = 2.40 vol% and  d ϕ  = 6.16 vol%.

sections.heading: FTIR analysis of the nanocomposites
paragraphs: The FTIR spectra of the pure PVA/PVP hybrid matrix and PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites were examined to determine the chemical interactions between the polymer matrix and the filler Fig.  2 . The pure PVA/PVP blend exhibits a weak O–H stretching peak around 3674 cm −1  and a broad hydroxyl band in the range of 3584–3060 cm −1 . This broad band reflects the strong hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl (–OH) groups of PVA and the carbonyl (C=O) groups of PVP [ 10 ,  40 ]. Upon the addition of GnP, a decrease in the bandwidth and a slight shift toward lower wavenumbers were observed, indicating that the filler induces a rearrangement of hydrogen bonds among the polymer chains [ 1 ,  14 ]. Figure 2 The FTIR spectra of pure PVA/PVP hybrid matrix and PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposite films.

Distinct bands observed at 2987 cm −1  and 2901 cm −1  correspond to the aliphatic C–H stretching vibrations in the PVA and PVP chains [ 10 ]. The variation in their intensity suggests that the local environment around the methylene groups changes due to the physical interactions between GnP and the polymer chains [ 5 ]. The sharp band at 1651 cm −1  is attributed to the carbonyl (C=O) stretching vibration of PVP and represents a characteristic feature of the PVA/PVP blend. This peak confirms the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds between the –OH groups of PVA and the C=O groups of PVP [ 10 ,  40 ]. A slight red shift of the 1651 cm −1  band with increasing GnP content indicates that the filler strengthens these interactions and facilitates bonding between polymer chains [ 1 ,  14 ].

The band at 1422 cm −1  corresponds to the symmetric bending vibration of CH 2  groups, while those at 1250 cm −1  and 1066 cm −1  are assigned to C–O–C and C–O stretching vibrations, respectively [ 12 ]. In particular, the C–O stretching band near 1066 cm −1  shows a slight shift upon GnP incorporation, supporting the presence of weak interactions (such as π–π or van der Waals forces) between the filler and the polymer chains [ 5 ,  40 ]. Additionally, the low-wavenumber bands observed at 772 cm −1  and 648 cm −1  are associated with C–C vibrations within the polymer backbone [ 14 ]. The sharpening of peaks in this region suggests that the highly ordered structure of GnP is successfully integrated into the PVA/PVP matrix.

The obtained FTIR results are in good agreement with those reported in the literature for other PVA/PVP-based nanocomposites [ 1 ,  5 ,  10 ,  12 ,  14 ,  40 ]. Specifically, the narrowing of the broad O–H band, the slight shift in the C=O stretching peak, and the changes in C–O vibrations indicate strong physical interactions between GnP and the polymer chains. These findings confirm that GnP exhibits good compatibility and strong interfacial interactions with the PVA/PVP matrix, thereby enhancing the structural integrity and homogeneity of the nanocomposite.

sections.heading: Electrical conductivity of the nanocomposites
UV–Vis analysis of the nanocomposites
paragraphs: UV–Vis absorption spectra, which provide detailed information about the optical behavior, optical parameters, and electronic band structures of materials, are very useful for investigating crystalline and amorphous polymeric materials [ 41 ,  42 ]. The absorbance ( A ) values of all nanocomposite samples measured in the wavelength range of 190–600 nm are presented in Fig. S2a. The pure PVA/PVP hybrid matrix exhibits low absorbance values across this range, indicating its transparency. All PVA/PVP–GnP samples show strong absorption in the 190–250 nm wavelength range, while absorbance remains nearly constant across the 250–600 nm range. The figure shows that absorbance increases below 250 nm for all film samples. Additionally, a strong absorbance peak associated with the π → π* transition appears at approximately 190 nm [ 4 ,  9 ]. As the GnP content in the composites increases, an absorbance peak around 260 nm becomes more pronounced. This small increase is attributed to GnPs in the composite structure acting as photon scattering centers. The figure also reveals that increasing the amount of GnP in the composites leads to higher absorbance levels.

The extinction coefficient ( k ), which represents the amount of energy lost due to light scattering and absorption in a material, defines the likelihood of electronic transitions within the material and is highly important for various optical and photonic applications [ 43 ,  44 ]. The variation of the extinction coefficient with wavelength for all samples is presented in Fig. S2b. It can be seen from the figure that as the wavelength decreases from higher values (visible region) to lower values (UV region), the extinction coefficient ( k ) initially exhibits a linear downward trend, followed by a noticeable increase in the range of 190–220 nm. This behavior is consistent with our previous findings reported in Mergen et al. [ 42 ]. As the volume fraction of the GnP filler in the composite increases, the absorption coefficient values increase accordingly, leading to greater energy loss [ 30 ]. Higher GnP doping in the PVA/PVP hybrid results in a significant increase in both the absorption and extinction coefficient values. In other words, the nanocomposites exhibit an enhanced capacity to absorb and dissipate electromagnetic energy, indicating that both absorption and extinction properties improve with increasing GnP concentration.

sections.heading: Determination of optical band gap energy
Determination of Urbach energy
Reflectance ( R ) and refractive index ( n )
paragraphs: The optical reflection spectra of all samples are presented in Fig.  7 a. In the visible region (350–600 nm), the reflectance values remain relatively stable for all compositions, indicating that the incorporation of GnPs does not significantly alter the optical response in this wavelength range. In contrast, a pronounced reflection maximum is observed in the ultraviolet region, centered at approximately 250 nm, which is consistent with the characteristic electronic transitions associated with the graphitic structure of GnPs [ 32 ,  46 ]. As clearly seen in the figure, the intensity of this UV reflection peak systematically increases with increasing GnP content in the PVA/PVP matrix. This behavior suggests that the graphitic nanoplatelets introduce an additional optically active phase, enhancing photon-material interactions at shorter wavelengths. The emergence and amplification of this maximum can be attributed to increased photon scattering and electronic transitions associated with the graphitic structure of GnPs, which become more effective as their volume fraction in the composite increases. Consequently, all PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites exhibit higher reflectance values compared to the pristine PVA/PVP hybrid matrix, with the highest reflectance observed for the sample containing the maximum GnP loading. Figure 7 a  The reflectance ( R ) and  b  The refractive index ( n ) spectra versus wavelength ( λ ) pure PVA/PVP hybrid matrix and PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites.

The refractive index ( n ) is a fundamental parameter for evaluating the optical properties of a material and shows the ratio of the speed of light in the vacuum to its speed within the material. This physical parameter is critically important for various applications, including the fabrication of optoelectronic devices, the selection of anti-reflective materials, and the design of optical filters and integrated devices [ 47 ,  48 ]. The refractive index defines the optical properties of a material by affecting light propagation, reflection, and absorbance coefficients. Fillers such as nanoparticles can increase the refractive index by increasing the density of composite films.

The variation of the refractive index values for all samples as a function of wavelength is shown in Fig.  7 b. As observed in the figure, the refractive index remains almost constant in the 350–600 nm region for all nanocomposites, but a rapid and significant increase is observed when the wavelength decreases below 350 nm. Notably, the addition of GnP nanoparticles into the PVA/PVP hybrid matrix leads to an increase in the refractive index values of the nanocomposites. The calculated refractive index values for different GnP concentrations at a constant wavelength of 400 nm are given in Table  1 .

An increase in filler content within the composite structure alters the internal arrangement of the polymer, leading to an enhancement in the refractive index. This increase is attributed to the changes in filler density and modifications in the polymer matrix structure [ 47 ,  49 ]. The incorporation of GnPs into the hybrid polymer matrix alters the packing density, resulting in variations in refractive index. Furthermore, the addition of GnPs introduces new defect sites within the composite, influencing both the density and polarizability of the material [ 50 ,  51 ]. These structural modifications reduce the transmission of light through the polymer composite, thereby explaining the observed increase in refractive index at higher filler volume fractions [ 49 ].

sections.heading: Optical conductivity
Optical dielectric study
Dispersion energy parameters
paragraphs: Another approach used to understand the optical behavior of materials and their interaction with light is to determine the dispersion energy parameters. Models such as the Wemple-DiDomenico (W-D) model, in particular, provide very important information about the electronic structure of materials [ 34 ,  39 ]. The W-D model finds extensive applications in fields such as optical material characterization, optical device design (e.g., filters, lenses, waveguides), photovoltaic applications, and dielectric/conductivity studies [ 26 ,  39 ,  44 ,  54 ]. It is a method used to investigate how a material's refractive index ( n ) changes with wavelength in the normal dispersion region, with the spectral dependence of the refractive index [ 26 ,  33 ,  34 – 35 ].

The Sellmeier oscillator model explains the relationship between the refractive index and wavelength based on oscillations arising from the interaction of light with atoms and molecules within the material [ 55 ]. In the one-term Sellmeier model, it is assumed that the largest contribution to the refractive index of the material comes from the oscillator with the lowest energy. Under this assumption, the oscillator equation becomes quite simple. It describes the wavelength dependence of the refractive index using parameters such as the average oscillator strength ( S o ) and the average oscillator wavelength (λ o ) [ 36 ,  56 ,  57 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The refractive index ( n ), optical conductivity σ opt , and dielectric constant of the nanocomposites have significantly improved depending on increasing GnP content. This structural transformation indicates that PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites hold significant promise for applications in optoelectronic and photonic devices. These findings support the potential use of PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites in communication systems and advanced photonic technologies.

The findings of this study underscore the versatility and promising potential of PVA/PVP–GnP nanocomposites for applications in energy storage systems, optoelectronic devices, and advanced optical technologies. Further studies are needed to investigate the long-term stability, scalability, and potential integration of these nanocomposites into commercial applications.
